newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia Gold-price fails to spark panic sales.
newsitem.headline: Australia Gold-price fails to spark panic sales.

text.p: Panic selling in the Australian gold market that followed the previous sharp drop in price has so far failed to materialise in response to the latest rout.
"We've been here before in terms of Aussie dollar and U.S. dollar gold," said a senior bullion dealer for an international bank.
"I don't think we're seeing the sort of panic we saw when gold came off two months ago to these levels," another bullion dealer said.
Dealers reasoned the lack of response reflects expections among investors that the gold price will recover.
Since gold touched a 46-month low in February of US$336.15 an ounce gold has staged a comeback to around US$360, dealers noted.
"People had a chance for some top-off hedging if they felt they missed the boat ... and so far on the move, people are just waiting to see what happens next, the dealer said.
"There's a bit of nervousness out there, but we're cetainly not seeing panic selling or buy backs of hedging positions."
COMEX June gold settled off 60 cents at US$343.30 an ounce on Wednesday after setting a new contract low US$337 earlier in the day.
In the bullion market in New York on Wednesday, spot gold ended quoted at US$341.00-$341.50 an ounce.
Bullion in Sydney was quoted late on Thursday at US$341.80 an ounce.
The Perth Mint quoted spot gold at A$442.21 an ounce, the lowest since the 1980s.
Australian gold producers are most sensitive to the Australian dollar price, although most are hedged forward at much higher prices.
"You would think the miners would be sweating," said a dealer. "But actually they seem content to use their existing hedging and ride this out."
Dealers said technical support around the 46-month low point was underpinning the market at the moment, although they voiced little confidence this level would not be breached.
A move below US$336 an ounce, could "pull out all the stops" leaving gold sharply lower into the weekend.
The latest fall in gold is being viewed as probably more related to hedge fund selling that any emerging perceptions of changes in the market's supply and demand fundamentals.
Suggestions by some overseas dealers that Germany's Bundesbank was preparing for a possible gold sale were discounted by the local market as a reason for gold's price fall.
"I don't think it was central bank selling," one dealer said.
"The banks have been willing to step back from the market below US$350," he said.
If the hedge funds are behind the selling, the potential for a correction on the upside soon was probably more likely, he added.
"But whether it's now or not until the price is a few dollars lower ... I'm not sure," the dealer said.
However, gold is not seen by many as a "good buy" currently, reflecting some sentiment in the market that gold has further to fall, the dealer added.
-- Melbourne bureau 61-3 9286-1421
